The Federalist Party. The first major political party in the United States, dominant from seventeen eighty-nine to the early eighteen hundreds, advocating for a strong central government and commercial development. Led by Alexander Hamilton and John Adams, it represented merchants, manufacturers, and coastal elites who believed national cohesion and economic strength required centralized federal authority. The party collapsed after the pivotal Election of eighteen hundred, when Thomas Jefferson and the rival Democratic-Republicans defeated them decisively.

The Federalist Party formed around Alexander Hamilton's compelling vision of a strong federal government with a national bank, tariffs, and active economic management. It backed ratification of the United States Constitution and won the nation's early elections throughout the seventeen nineties. The party supported John Adams throughout his presidency from seventeen ninety-seven to eighteen oh-one, during which Federalists passed the controversial Alien and Sedition Acts to suppress dissent. It was opposed by Thomas Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans, who favored state power and agrarian interests. The party collapsed irreversibly after the Election of eighteen hundred, when Jefferson defeated Adams and the party fragmented into irrelevance. Its core ideas—a strong executive, fiscal responsibility, and federal commercial power—influenced American conservatism for centuries. It drew strong support from merchants, shipowners, and urban commercial interests; opposed by farmers and southern planters who deeply feared federal intrusion on state autonomy. The Federalists promoted a strong national military, a national debt as an economic tool, and protective tariffs to build American manufacturing independence and shield the nation from foreign economic domination. The party's demise after eighteen hundred did not end its ideology: Federalist principles of energetic central government and commercial capitalism deeply influenced later Republican parties and American statecraft throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The Federalist Party connects to the Democratic-Republican Party as the rival faction that defeated the Federalists in the eighteen hundred election; Alexander Hamilton as the party's intellectual architect and most forceful organizer; John Adams as the party's presidential leader during its period of dominance; the Alien and Sedition Acts as the controversial legislation Federalists enacted to strengthen federal power and suppress dissent; the Election of eighteen hundred as the pivotal election that ended Federalist supremacy; and Thomas Jefferson as the Democratic-Republican who defeated the Federalists and reshaped the nation's political course.
